https://www.dw.com/en/what-would-an-afd-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Kvfv Ulrich Siegmund, top candidate for the far-right AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, is confident he will get the mandate to form a government Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS Advertisement The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt . The far-right party, currently way ahead in opinion polls, is hoping to form a single-party government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund , serve as state premier. The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right." Radical tightening of asylum laws In its draft government program , the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible. The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry." What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a " Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy. Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law. And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state. Anti-immigration policy The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt. However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers , particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back. To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program." Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today. Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage . "Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions." Rapprochement with Russia The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight. For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022 , Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions. The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat. Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose. On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy. Establishing citizen patrols Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture." Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online . Germany's freedom of art under threat? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote. Radical change in social policy A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly. It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy." To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments. Subscribe ITV News Anglia reports that two Latvian men, aged 32 and 26, have been released on bail after an arrest inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire. They were detained at 2am on Thursday after police found a small hole in the perimeter fence. - Advertisement - Police later carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area, and Commander Helen Flanagan said the inquiry is still focused on why the men were at the site. RAF Molesworth is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence work. RAF Molesworth arrest Military police found an abandoned vehicle near RAF Molesworth at around 10pm on Wednesday, about four hours before the arrests. The vehicle was taken to a nearby police location, and officers from Cambridgeshire police joined the search after the fence damage was identified. The men were first arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. Police then arrested them again on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, which covers entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK. Helen Flanagan investigation Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said there was nothing from the inquiry so far to suggest a connection to an incident near RAF Fairford in September. She also said the force was “very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites”. - Advertisement - Flanagan added: “Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence police and Cambridgeshire constabulary on this. A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity,” Peterborough searches The bail conditions keep the case active while police continue to examine motive and possible criminal activity. The two searches in the Peterborough area suggest the inquiry has moved beyond the gate breach itself and into the men’s wider movements and any evidence linked to their entry. For now, the immediate change is simple: the two Latvians are out on bail, but the investigation has not closed. The unanswered issue is why they were inside RAF Molesworth at all.
